190.title: The caliph finds him
190.hook: Caliph Umar, sent by a dream, brings him gold, and the harper weeps at being seen (Masnavi 1)
190.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, stories like this one are read as a picture of God noticing the forgotten, and many readers take it as a reason to look for the people others pass by.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in the days of Umar, an old harper walked out to the graveyard and played for God alone. Play for no one.

Being noticed when nobody seemed to be looking can be a strange thing. The teacher who stopped you in the hall to say she'd read what you wrote. The boss who remembered the thing you did quietly months ago. A stranger who saw you were struggling and just asked. Someone can hold it together for years, and one person really seeing them is what brings the tears. The old harper is asleep on a grave, his harp for a pillow. Somebody is on the way.
screen: `NOTICED WHEN NOBODY WAS LOOKING.` → `ASLEEP ON A GRAVE.` → `THE CALIPH FINDS HIM.`

segments.voice: While the harper sleeps, the caliph Umar also falls asleep, and a voice comes to him in a dream. A servant of God is lying in the graveyard, it says: take seven hundred gold dinars from the treasury and bring them to him. Umar goes. He walks the whole graveyard and sees nobody but an old man asleep. Surely not him. He circles again. Still only the old man. Then it dawns on him: this is the one. So the caliph himself stands over a worn-out musician, the kind of man people pass without a glance, and waits by him until he stirs. The harper opens his eyes, sees the caliph, and starts to shake. He assumes he's in trouble. Umar tells him not to be afraid; he has come with good news. God sends greetings, and this gold, and there's more when it runs out. That's when the harper breaks. He weeps, and in Rumi's telling he flings his harp down and smashes it, crying out that it had stood between him and God. He mourns all the years he spent performing. The gold barely matters. What undoes him is that he was seen. Sufi readers take the heart of the story to be this: the one nobody wanted, playing to empty graves, had an audience after all. Your line: you were seen.
screen: `A DREAM, AND SEVEN HUNDRED DINARS.` · `SURELY NOT HIM.` · `THE HARPER SHAKES, THEN WEEPS.` · then, large: `YOU WERE SEEN.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who gets passed by: the person who cleans the building, the quiet cousin, the neighbor who lives alone, an older relative who doesn't get many calls. Hold them in mind with no plan, and just see them, the way Umar finally saw the old man on the grave. If you pray, you can hold them there too.
Khalifa. The Arabic word for caliph, the leader of the Muslim community; Umar, who found the old harper, was the second. Today's word.
Your line: you were seen. Seven hundred dinars mattered less than that. That's day one hundred ninety.

191.title: Past the veil
191.hook: the harper is told even his regret about the past is a veil to move beyond (Masnavi 1)
191.howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, repentance matters, but teachers often warn against getting stuck in regret; the goal described in stories like this is fana, a passing away of the self-centered self.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the khalifa found the old harper in the graveyard, and he wept at being noticed. You were seen.

Some people apologize for the same thing for twenty years. The friend who still brings up how she behaved at her sister's wedding. The dad who can't stop saying he worked too much when the kids were small. The regret is real, and it was once useful. But at some point the regret itself becomes the thing they carry, heavier than whatever happened. The old harper is still on the grave, weeping over his whole life. The caliph is about to say something surprising about those tears.
screen: `THE SAME APOLOGY FOR TWENTY YEARS.` → `THE HARPER, WEEPING.` → `PAST THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: The harper is mourning his seventy years of music, the harp he just smashed, all the breath he spent on other people. You'd expect Umar to praise him: finally, real repentance. Instead, in Rumi's telling, Umar says this weeping is also a sign that you're still awake to yourself. Your eyes are still on the past. And the past and the future are veils between you and God. Burn them both. How long will you stay tied up in these knots? A veil, in Rumi's language, is anything that hangs between you and what's real. Pride can be a veil. So can shame. The harper had moved from one to the other: first proud of his voice, now sorry about it. Either way, the story is still about him. Umar invites him one step further, past both. Rumi says the harper's heart woke up. He stopped weeping, and he stopped laughing too. He went into a state Rumi says can't be described, and the poem simply lets him go. Sufis call this passing away of the small self fana. The point doesn't depend on the word: there comes a time when even your regrets are just more ways of staring at yourself. Rumi isn't saying the past doesn't matter. He's saying you can't live facing backward. And that brings the week together: the parrot that played dead to get free, Marcus's inner retreat, change as nature's favorite thing, and an old man who played for no one, was seen, and walked past the veil. Your line: past the veil.
screen: `EVEN YOUR TEARS ARE STILL ABOUT YOU.` · `PAST AND FUTURE ARE VEILS.` · `NO WEEPING, NO LAUGHING.` · then, large: `PAST THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: Find one thing you keep holding against yourself, something old, not something that still needs fixing, and look at it plainly for a breath or two. Then imagine setting it down beside you, the way the harper finally put his weeping down. You're not pretending it didn't happen; you're just not carrying it for the next two minutes.
Fana. The Sufi term for the passing away of the small self, which Umar invites the weeping harper toward. Today's word.
Your line: burn them both. Even regret can become one more veil. That's the week.

192.title: Like the vine
192.hook: a vine gives grapes and asks nothing more, so do good and move on (Meditations 5.6)
192.carry: giving grapes is what vines do
192.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus often use this passage as a check on their own motives, and many traditions share a version of the idea that good done quietly, without keeping score, is good done well.

segments.voice: Last week ended with the old harper walking past even his own regret, past the veil. Burn them both.

You hold the door for someone and they don't say thanks. And there it is: a tiny flash of annoyance. Or you help a friend move, carry the couch down three flights, and a month later you're still keeping score, just a little. Plenty of people do good things and then hang around the good thing, waiting for it to be noticed. A new week starts today, called the shepherd, for a story coming in two days. But first, Marcus has a picture for that little scorekeeper. It grows on a trellis.
screen: `NO THANKS FOR THE DOOR.` → `STILL KEEPING SCORE.` → `LIKE THE VINE.`

segments.voice: In Book Five of the Meditations, Marcus sorts people who do good into three kinds. The first does you a favor and is ready to send the bill: you owe me. The second asks for nothing out loud, but quietly thinks of you as in their debt, and knows exactly what they did. The third, Marcus says, in a way doesn't even know what he has done. He's like a vine that has produced grapes and asks for nothing more once it has borne its own fruit. Then Marcus piles up more pictures: a horse that has run its race, a dog that has tracked the game, a bee that has made its honey. None of them calls everyone over to look. They go on to the next thing, the way the vine, next season, simply makes grapes again. That's doing good as part of your nature, not a transaction. Marcus imagines someone objecting: surely a decent person should notice what they've done? He grants the point, then warns that this is how you slide back into the first kind of person. The vine isn't being humble. Being humble would still be about the vine. It's just being a vine. For Marcus, being helpful is what a human being is for, so helping isn't a favor you've done anyone. It's you working properly, and the reward is already in it, the way the grapes are already the vine's whole point. Your line: giving grapes is what vines do.
screen: `THREE KINDS OF PEOPLE WHO DO GOOD.` · `A VINE THAT ASKS NOTHING MORE.` · `THE HORSE, THE DOG, THE BEE.` · then, large: `LIKE THE VINE.`

segments.voice: Think of one small thing you could do for someone: refill something, fix something, send something, take a chore off someone's list. Picture yourself doing it, then walking away without saying a word. Notice the part of you that wants credit, let it be there, and breathe.
Vine, Marcus's picture of the best kind of good: it gives its grapes and asks for nothing more, then does it again next season. Today's word.
Your line: giving grapes is what vines do. No bill, and no score kept. Until tomorrow.

193.title: The mind is dyed
193.hook: your mind takes the color of the thoughts you keep (Meditations 5.16)
193.howItsDone: Many readers of the Stoics keep a few short lines to return to through the day, and some write them on cards or repeat them at set times, the way Marcus repeated his own reminders.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus's vine gave its grapes and asked for nothing more. Giving grapes is what vines do.

Drop a white T-shirt into a pot of hot water with one red sock. It doesn't take much, and it doesn't take long. Everything comes out pink. Now run through the thoughts that go round in your head on a normal day. The comment someone made at work. The worry about money. The replay of an argument you already lost. Or the song you love, the kid's joke, the thing you're grateful for. You don't choose every thought that shows up. But some of them you keep in the water, over and over. Marcus noticed what that does.
screen: `ONE RED SOCK.` → `THE THOUGHTS YOU KEEP IN THE WATER.` → `THE MIND IS DYED.`

segments.voice: Here's the line from Book Five, in George Long's translation: "Such as are thy habitual thoughts, such also will be the character of thy mind; for the soul is dyed by the thoughts." Dyed is a strong word. Dye that takes doesn't sit on the surface. The color goes all the way through and won't wash out. It isn't what you think once that shapes you. It's what you think habitually, the thoughts you dip into every day. So Marcus tells himself to dye his soul on purpose, with a steady run of good thoughts, and gives an example. Where a person can live, he says, they can also live well. Then he tests it on himself. Someone might say, but I have to live in a palace. Fine, he answers: a person can live well in a palace, too. Remember who's writing. The palace was his actual address. He isn't dreaming of a quiet cabin. He's telling himself that the life he's stuck with can still be lived well, because the color of it comes from inside. Psychologists today have a name, rumination, for a thought on repeat. Marcus used the picture of a dye pot. You can't stop every thought from coming. You can choose which ones you keep dipping into. Your line: dyed by thoughts.
screen: `THE SOUL IS DYED BY THE THOUGHTS.` · `DYED ALL THE WAY THROUGH.` · `YOU CAN LIVE WELL IN A PALACE, TOO.` · then, large: `DYED BY THOUGHTS.`

segments.voice: Let a few of your usual thoughts go by, and notice which ones come back most. Then choose one you'd like to soak in instead, something true and steadying: I can live well even here, or this day is enough, or a line from a text you love. Say it slowly inside, a few times, and let it sink in.
Rumination, the name for a thought on repeat, like Marcus's picture of a mind dyed by the thoughts it keeps returning to. Today's word.
Your line: dyed by thoughts. The color goes all the way through. Day one hundred ninety-three.

194.title: Moses and the shepherd
194.hook: a shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and Moses scolds him (Masnavi 2.1720ff)
194.howItsDone: Alongside set prayers, many traditions make room for personal prayer in a person's own words, and readers of Rumi often point to this story when they talk about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Marcus said the soul is dyed by the thoughts it keeps. Dyed by thoughts.

Listen to a small child pray at bedtime. Thank you for the dog. Please make Grandma's knee better. Are you cold up there? Adults sometimes smile, and sometimes wince a little: that's not how you talk to God. There's a right way, isn't there? The proper words, the ones in the book. Rumi tells a story about exactly this, in the Masnavi. It's the story this week is named for, and it takes three days. It begins with a man alone on a hillside with his goats.
screen: `ARE YOU COLD UP THERE?` → `THE PROPER WORDS.` → `MOSES AND THE SHEPHERD.`

segments.voice: It's in Book Two. Moses, honored as a prophet in Judaism, Christianity and Islam, is walking along a road when he hears a shepherd praying out loud, something like this. God, where are you? Let me be your servant. I'd mend your shoes and comb your hair. I'd wash your clothes and pick out your lice. I'd bring you milk. I'd kiss your little hand and rub your little feet, and sweep out the place where you sleep at night. All my goats are yours. This man has no learning. He's offering God the only things he knows how to give: the care you'd give someone you love who's tired and far from home. Moses stops. Who are you talking to? The shepherd says: the one who made us, and made the earth and sky. Moses is horrified. In Rumi's telling, he tells the shepherd he's talking nonsense, that he should stuff cotton in his mouth, that God has no need of shoes and socks and milk. Talk like that, Moses says, is fit for a body that grows and needs feeding, not for God. Moses isn't wrong about God; Rumi's tradition teaches that God has no body. But watch what the scolding does. The shepherd says, you've shut my mouth and set my soul on fire with regret. He tears his clothes, lets out a long sigh, turns, and walks away into the desert. What God thinks comes tomorrow. For today, just notice the prayer itself, clumsy and completely sincere. Your line: in your own words.
screen: `A SHEPHERD PRAYS OUT LOUD.` · `I'D COMB YOUR HAIR AND WASH YOUR FEET.` · `MOSES: GOD NEEDS NO SHOES.` · then, large: `IN YOUR OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let one or two things you're grateful for today come to mind, and say thank you for them inside, in the plainest words you've got: thanks for the coffee, thanks that the test came back fine. No borrowed phrases, nothing you'd put in a card. If you pray, you can say it to God; if not, just say it into the quiet.
Shepherd. A shepherd prays to comb God's hair and wash God's feet, and the prophet Moses scolds him for it. Today's word.
Your line: in your own words. Clumsy can still be sincere. The story goes on tomorrow.

195.title: Moses is rebuked
195.hook: a voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them (Masnavi 2)
195.howItsDone: Readers of Rumi often cite this story when they talk about respecting other people's ways of prayer, and many Sufi teachers use it to warn against judging sincerity by vocabulary.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Moses scolded a shepherd for offering to comb God's hair, and the shepherd walked off into the desert. In your own words.

Maybe you've been corrected at a moment you were trying your hardest. You cooked for someone and they told you how their mother makes it. You finally opened up about something and got a lecture back. The correction might even have been right. But something closed, and it didn't open again for a long time. Moses, presumably, walked on feeling he'd done his job. Then he hears a voice, and it isn't pleased with him.
screen: `CORRECTED WHILE TRYING YOUR HARDEST.` → `SOMETHING CLOSED.` → `MOSES IS REBUKED.`

segments.voice: In Rumi's telling, a revelation comes to Moses from God, something like this. You have parted my servant from me. Did you come as a prophet to bring people together, or to split them apart? Rumi puts it in a rhyming couplet: you came to unite, not to sever. Then the voice goes on. I have given every person a way of their own, a way of speaking. What is praise from him would be blame from you. What's honey for one is poison for another. And then the turn: I don't look at the tongue and the words. I look at the heart and its state. Rumi gives an example from his own world: the idiom of India is praise for the people of India, the idiom of Sind for the people of Sind. Different words, the same longing. Notice what the story doesn't say. It doesn't say Moses was wrong that God has no body; Rumi's tradition keeps that teaching. It says Moses was wrong to make the shepherd's words the test of his heart. The man's language was mistaken. His love was not. That's hard for anyone who loves getting things right. The story isn't against correct teaching. It's a warning about what correction can cost when it lands on someone who is only trying to love. So when you hear someone pray or talk about the sacred in a way that isn't yours, the story suggests a first thought: their words, not mine.
screen: `YOU HAVE PARTED MY SERVANT FROM ME.` · `YOU CAME TO UNITE, NOT TO SEVER.` · `I LOOK AT THE HEART, NOT THE TONGUE.` · then, large: `THEIR WORDS, NOT MINE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone whose way with the sacred is different from yours: a grandmother with her beads, a friend who talks to the universe, a colleague who fasts, a child at bedtime. Picture them in the middle of it, and don't correct anything, even inside. Just listen for the heart underneath the words.
Vasl, Persian for union: the voice tells Moses he was sent to join people to God, not to part them, and that God looks at the heart, not the tongue. Today's word.
Your line: their words, not mine. God looks at the heart. Day one hundred ninety-five, done.

196.title: Beyond words
196.hook: Moses runs after the shepherd, who has gone past speech altogether (Masnavi 2)
196.howItsDone: Many traditions keep a practice of silent prayer or contemplation alongside spoken prayer, and some of Rumi's lyric poems close on the word for silent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vasl: God told Moses he was sent to unite, not to sever. Their words, not mine.

Running after someone to apologize goes like this. Out the door, down the street, heart going, rehearsing the words. And sometimes, on catching up, it turns out they've already moved on. Not in anger. They've just gone somewhere that can't quite be followed anymore. Moses has been rebuked. He knows he has to find the shepherd and set things right. So the prophet goes out into the desert, running. Today, the last part of the story.
screen: `RUNNING AFTER SOMEONE TO APOLOGIZE.` → `INTO THE DESERT.` → `BEYOND WORDS.`

segments.voice: Rumi gives a lovely detail. Moses follows the shepherd's footprints in the sand, and they're all over the place: the steps of someone lost in his own heart, one like a castle on a chessboard, going straight, another like a bishop, going slantwise. Finally Moses catches up, with good news. You have permission, he says. Don't look for rules or proper forms. Say whatever your heart wants to say. Your way of praying is the light of faith. It sounds like the happy ending. It isn't. The shepherd answers: Moses, I've gone past that now. I'm soaked in my heart's blood. In Rumi's telling he has passed beyond the Lote Tree, the tree that in Islamic tradition marks the farthest boundary of heaven. You struck my horse with your whip, he tells Moses, and it leapt and went beyond the sky. And then: my state now is beyond telling. What I'm saying to you isn't my state. The scolding didn't just hurt him. It pushed him past the need for words altogether. Then Rumi turns to the reader. Whatever you say in praise of God, he says, is like the image a mirror shows. The picture is yours, not the mirror's. On Rumi's reading, words about the sacred are never the sacred itself. Even the proper ones. Even Moses's. Yesterday was about not judging someone's words. Today goes one step further: at the deepest point, maybe no words fit. Your line: soaked in my heart's blood.
screen: `FOOTPRINTS LIKE CHESS PIECES.` · `YOU HAVE PERMISSION.` · `I'VE GONE PAST THAT NOW.` · then, large: `BEYOND WORDS.`

segments.voice: Let the words in your head slow down, the way traffic thins late at night; when a sentence starts, you don't have to finish it, just let it trail off. Rest in whatever is there before the words. If you pray, this can be a prayer with nothing said.
Beyond words. Moses runs after the shepherd to give him permission to pray his own way, and finds he has gone past speech altogether. Today's word.
Your line: soaked in my heart's blood. Some things are bigger than words. That's day one hundred ninety-six.

I've gone past that now; my state is beyond telling.
fork.reveal: the shepherd says the scolding sent him beyond the sky, and that what he says is no longer his state.

original.note: Persian: silent, hushed. some of Rumi's lyric poems close on this word.

trapdoor: what you thought: the shepherd gets his old prayer back.
what it means: he has gone past needing words at all.
what a scholar hears: the Lote Tree, sidrat al-muntaha, the boundary of heaven in the Qur'an and the Prophet's night journey, and the ghazals of Rumi that close on khamush, 'be silent'.
guess: past the point where speech can say it
a prayer said silently in your head
something too secret to tell anyone

sources.work: The Qur'an (the Lote Tree of the utmost boundary, described)
